(CNN) -- After weeks of controversy over Michael Mukasey's views on waterboarding, the Senate late Thursday approved the former judge's nomination for attorney general by a 53-40 vote. Waterboarding threatened to derail the approval of President Bush's nominee to lead the Justice Department. President Bush nominated Mukasey to replace longtime ally Alberto Gonzales, who resigned in September. The nomination had been considered at risk after a number of Democratic senators opposed Mukasey because of questions that arose from his views on the terror interrogation technique known as waterboarding and the president's power to order electronic surveillance. Mukasey, a former federal judge in New York, told senators he considers waterboarding "repugnant," but he could not categorically say whether the technique amounts to torture, which U.S. and international law bans. Waterboarding is a technique that involves restraining a suspect and pouring water on him to produce the sensation of drowning. Mukasey's confirmation was all but assured last week when two key Democrats on the Senate Judiciary Committee -- Sens. Dianne Feinstein of California and Chuck Schumer of New York -- said they would vote in favor of Mukasey despite the controversy. "The Department of Justice, once the crown jewel among government institutions, is adrift and rudderless," Schumer said Tuesday -- the same day the committee voted 11-8 to send Mukasey's nomination to the Senate floor. "It desperately needs a strong and independent leader at the helm to set it back on course and I believe Judge Mukasey is that person." Schumer said that in a meeting Friday the nominee said that Congress would be within its rights to pass a law that bans waterboarding across all government agencies and that the president "would have absolutely no legal authority to ignore" it. Schumer said he believed Mukasey would be more likely to find waterboarding illegal than an interim attorney general. "Indeed, his written answers to our notices have demonstrated more openness to ending the practices we abhor than either of this president's previous attorney general nominees have." But Mukasey's pledge to enforce such a law rang hollow with Sen. Patrick Leahy, D-Vermont, the Judiciary Committee's chairman. "Some have sought to find comfort in Judge Mukasey's personal assurance that he would enforce a future, new law against waterboarding if this Congress were to pass one," Leahy said Tuesday. "Unsaid, of course, is the fact that any such prohibition would have to be enacted over the veto of this president." However, the committee's ranking Republican, Sen. Arlen Specter of Pennsylvania, said he believed Mukasey would enforce a law banning waterboarding. "He could have said a lot of things which would have given me more assurances," Specter said earlier. "But he is intelligent; he's really learned in the law. He's strong, ethical, honest beyond any question. He's not an intimate of the president." A majority of Americans consider waterboarding a form of torture, but some of those say it's OK for the U.S. government to use the technique, according to a poll released Tuesday. Asked whether they think waterboarding is a form of torture, more than two-thirds of respondents, or 69 percent, said yes; 29 percent said no. Asked whether they think the U.S. government should be allowed to use the procedure to try to get information from suspected terrorists, 58 percent said no; 40 percent said yes. The CNN/Opinion Research Corp. telephone poll of 1,024 American adults was carried out over the weekend and had a sampling error of plus or minus 4.5 percentage points. E-mail to a friend .

(CNN) — Following weeks of debate about Michael Mukasey’s position on waterboarding, the Senate voted 53-40 late Thursday to confirm the former federal judge as attorney general.

The dispute over the interrogation method had put President Bush’s choice to head the Justice Department in jeopardy. Bush selected Mukasey to succeed his longtime associate Alberto Gonzales, who stepped down in September.

Several Democratic senators opposed the nomination after concerns emerged about Mukasey’s views on waterboarding and on the president’s authority to authorize electronic surveillance. Mukasey, who previously served as a federal judge in New York, told lawmakers that he found waterboarding “repugnant.” However, he declined to state unequivocally that it constitutes torture, which is prohibited under both U.S. and international law.

Waterboarding involves immobilizing a detainee and pouring water over him to create the feeling that he is drowning.

Mukasey’s confirmation became virtually certain the previous week after two influential Democrats on the Senate Judiciary Committee—California Sen. Dianne Feinstein and New York Sen. Chuck Schumer—announced that they would support him despite the controversy.

On Tuesday, the same day the committee voted 11-8 to advance the nomination to the full Senate, Schumer said the Justice Department had lost direction despite once being considered one of the federal government’s premier institutions. He argued that the department urgently required a capable, independent leader and that Mukasey was the right person to restore it.

Schumer also said Mukasey had told him during a Friday meeting that Congress had the constitutional authority to enact a government-wide prohibition on waterboarding. According to Schumer, Mukasey further stated that the president would have no lawful power to disregard such a ban.

In Schumer’s view, Mukasey was more likely than an acting attorney general to conclude that waterboarding was illegal. He added that Mukasey’s written responses showed greater willingness to halt practices Democrats opposed than the responses given by either of President Bush’s previous nominees for attorney general.

Sen. Patrick Leahy of Vermont, the Democratic chairman of the Judiciary Committee, was not persuaded by Mukasey’s promise to enforce a future ban. On Tuesday, Leahy said some lawmakers had taken reassurance from Mukasey’s personal commitment to uphold a new anti-waterboarding law if Congress passed one. Leahy noted, however, that such legislation would likely have to become law despite a presidential veto.

Pennsylvania Sen. Arlen Specter, the committee’s senior Republican, said he believed Mukasey would carry out a law prohibiting waterboarding. Specter acknowledged that Mukasey could have made statements offering stronger reassurance, but described him as intelligent, deeply knowledgeable about the law, strong, ethical and unquestionably honest. He also pointed out that Mukasey was not personally close to the president.

A poll released Tuesday found that most Americans regarded waterboarding as torture, although some respondents who held that view still approved of its use by the U.S. government.

When asked whether waterboarding should be classified as torture, 69 percent said it should, while 29 percent disagreed. In a separate question about whether the government should be permitted to use the method to obtain information from suspected terrorists, 58 percent opposed its use and 40 percent supported it.

The CNN/Opinion Research Corp. survey questioned 1,024 American adults by telephone over the weekend. Its sampling error was plus or minus 4.5 percentage points.

# Senate Confirms Mukasey as Attorney General Despite Waterboarding Dispute

**WASHINGTON, Nov. 8, 2007 —** The Senate confirmed retired federal judge Michael B. Mukasey as attorney general Thursday night, overcoming opposition from most Democrats who criticized his refusal to declare waterboarding illegal and questioned his views on presidential surveillance powers.

The vote was **53-40**, giving President George W. Bush a new attorney general following the resignation of Alberto R. Gonzales. Mukasey prevailed with near-unanimous Republican support and backing from a small group of Democrats, including Sens. Charles E. Schumer of New York and Dianne Feinstein of California.

Those two Democrats had already helped advance Mukasey’s nomination through the Senate Judiciary Committee on an 11-8 vote. They argued that, despite serious reservations, Mukasey was preferable to leaving the Justice Department under temporary leadership and could restore independence and credibility after the controversies surrounding Gonzales.

Mukasey’s confirmation became uncertain after he declined during his hearings and in subsequent written answers to say whether waterboarding—a harsh interrogation technique that simulates drowning—constitutes torture and is therefore illegal. He called the technique repugnant but said he lacked access to the classified details needed to make a legal judgment.

That explanation did not satisfy Democratic leaders and human-rights advocates, who said existing U.S. law and treaty obligations clearly prohibit waterboarding. They warned that confirming Mukasey without an unequivocal answer could weaken legal barriers against torture.

Democrats also challenged Mukasey over the Bush administration’s claims of broad executive authority, particularly its warrantless surveillance program. Critics said his answers left open the possibility that a president could disregard statutes during wartime. Mukasey maintained that the president must obey the Constitution and said he would enforce laws enacted by Congress, but he avoided categorical conclusions about classified surveillance operations.

Republicans defended Mukasey as a highly qualified and independent former judge who should not be required to issue legal opinions without reviewing classified facts. Supporters also pointed to his pledges not to authorize conduct he found unlawful and to resign rather than carry out an illegal presidential order.

The limited Democratic support proved decisive. With Republicans largely united, the crossover votes gave Mukasey the majority needed for confirmation despite opposition from Judiciary Committee Chairman Patrick Leahy and other senior Democrats.

Mukasey, a former chief judge of the federal district court in Manhattan, will take control of a Justice Department strained by disputes over political influence, the dismissal of U.S. attorneys, interrogation policy and domestic surveillance.

Democratic senators Charles Schumer and Dianne Feinstein joined Republicans to advance the nomination, producing an **11–8 committee vote**.
- **Senate vote:** The full Senate confirmed Mukasey on November 8, 2007, by **53–40**, a relatively narrow margin for an attorney-general nominee. **Senate confirms Mukasey as attorney general despite dispute over waterboarding**  
*November 8, 2007 — Washington*

The Senate confirmed Michael B. Mukasey as attorney general Thursday night, approving President George W. Bush’s nominee by a 53-40 vote after a contentious debate dominated by Mukasey’s refusal to say unequivocally whether waterboarding constitutes torture.

Mukasey, a retired federal judge and former prosecutor, will replace Alberto Gonzales, who resigned in September amid congressional investigations into the dismissal of U.S. attorneys and allegations that the Justice Department had become politicized.

Most Republicans supported the nomination. Six Democrats—Evan Bayh of Indiana, Tom Carper of Delaware, Dianne Feinstein of California, Mary Landrieu of Louisiana, Ben Nelson of Nebraska and Charles Schumer of New York—also voted for Mukasey. Independent Sen. Joseph Lieberman of Connecticut joined them.

The confirmation followed a 53-38 vote to end debate and bring the nomination to a final vote.

### Waterboarding dominates the debate

Mukasey’s nomination initially drew bipartisan praise. As chief judge of the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, he had presided over major terrorism cases and was widely described as independent and experienced.

Support began to erode, however, after his confirmation hearings before the Senate Judiciary Committee. Asked whether waterboarding—the simulated-drowning interrogation technique used by the CIA on some terrorism suspects—was torture, Mukasey declined to give a definitive answer.

In written responses to senators, Mukasey called waterboarding “repugnant to me” and said torture is illegal. But he maintained that he lacked access to classified details about the technique and could not offer a legal judgment without knowing how it had been used and what Justice Department opinions already existed.

That answer angered Democrats and some human-rights advocates, who argued that waterboarding has long been recognized as torture under U.S. and international law.

Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Patrick Leahy, D-Vermont, opposed the nomination, saying Mukasey had failed a fundamental test.

“Judge Mukasey’s unwillingness to say that waterboarding is illegal is deeply troubling,” Leahy said during the debate. He argued that the next attorney general must be willing to reject unlawful interrogation practices rather than defer to secret executive-branch legal opinions.

Sen. Edward Kennedy, D-Massachusetts, was more direct, declaring: “Waterboarding is torture.” He said confirming a nominee who would not acknowledge that fact would weaken the United States’ moral and legal standing.

Sen. John McCain, R-Arizona, a former prisoner of war and a leading congressional opponent of abusive interrogations, also has repeatedly described waterboarding as torture, although he did not cast a vote in Thursday’s final tally.

### Schumer and Feinstein provide decisive support

Mukasey’s prospects improved when Schumer and Feinstein, both Judiciary Committee Democrats, announced they would support him. Their votes allowed the nomination to clear the committee and helped secure confirmation in the full Senate.

Schumer, who had initially recommended Mukasey to the White House as a possible consensus nominee, called the decision “an extremely difficult vote.”

He said Mukasey’s answers on waterboarding were unsatisfactory but argued that the nominee remained preferable to continued leadership by an acting attorney general closely aligned with the White House.

“Judge Mukasey is not my ideal nominee,” Schumer said, but added that he believed Mukasey would be “a significant improvement over Alberto Gonzales” and would be more independent than other candidates President Bush might select if the nomination failed.

Feinstein similarly said she was disappointed by Mukasey’s refusal to classify waterboarding as torture but concluded that rejecting him would not necessarily produce a nominee more willing to challenge the administration.

“I believe he is the best nominee we are going to get from this administration,” Feinstein said.

Republican supporters defended Mukasey’s caution, saying it would have been improper for him to issue a legal judgment without access to classified facts or the relevant Justice Department memoranda.

Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell, R-Kentucky, said Mukasey had demonstrated independence, legal ability and a commitment to restoring confidence in the Justice Department. Republicans also accused Democrats of turning the nomination into a referendum on interrogation policies rather than judging Mukasey’s broader qualifications.

### Poll finds broad public agreement that waterboarding is torture

The Senate debate came as a CNN/Opinion Research Corp. poll showed that most Americans considered waterboarding to be torture.

In the survey, conducted November 2-4 among 1,024 adults, **69 percent said waterboarding constitutes torture**, while **29 percent said it does not**. The poll had a sampling error of approximately plus or minus three percentage points.

The public was somewhat more divided when asked whether the government should be permitted to use waterboarding to obtain information from suspected terrorists. **Fifty-eight percent said it should not be allowed, while 40 percent said it should be permitted.**

The results underscored the political risk surrounding the issue: although a clear majority classified the technique as torture, a substantial minority still supported its use under some circumstances.

### Bush welcomes confirmation

President Bush had strongly defended Mukasey, warning that failure to confirm him would leave the Justice Department without permanent leadership at a time of continuing terrorism threats.

The White House also maintained that the United States does not torture, while refusing to discuss specific interrogation techniques or acknowledge which methods had been authorized for the CIA.

Mukasey has pledged that, once confirmed and given access to classified information, he will review the government’s interrogation policies and enforce any law enacted by Congress. He also said the president cannot authorize violations of federal statutes simply by invoking wartime powers.

His first major challenge will be restoring morale and credibility at the Justice Department after months of controversy under Gonzales. He will also inherit disputes over domestic surveillance, executive privilege, the treatment of terrorism suspects and congressional demands for documents and testimony from administration officials.

Mukasey is expected to be sworn in as the 81st attorney general on Friday.
